one_liner: Header-only C/C++ 32-bit remainder, division and divisibility by a reused divisor (LKK direct remainder); about 3x faster than hardware div.
what_it_does: Computes a % d, a / d and 'is a divisible by d' for 32-bit unsigned and signed integers when the same divisor is used many times, such as a hash-table bucket count chosen at run time. You call computeM_u32(d) (or computeM_s32) once to get a 64-bit magic number M, then fastmod_u32(a, M, d), fastdiv_u32(a, M) or is_divisible(a, M) per operation; in C++ the functions are constexpr (C++14, not on MSVC) and fastmod<d>/fastdiv<d> templates exist. It does not replace the % operator transparently: you carry M and d yourself. Experimental unsigned 64-bit versions use a 128-bit M.
how_it_is_fast: It implements the Lemire-Kaser-Kurz (LKK) direct remainder: with M = ceil(2^64/d), the low 64 bits of M*a hold the fractional part of a/d, and the high 64 bits of that fraction times d are a % d. A remainder therefore costs two multiplications (one of them a 64x64 high product) instead of a divide instruction, and skips the quotient-multiply-subtract sequence compilers emit for constant divisors. Division is the high half of M*a, and divisibility is one multiply and compare (a*M <= M-1). The 64-bit variants need 128-bit M and products, and the header itself warns they may not beat compiler code.
when_to_use: Hash tables, sharding or hash/LCG steps where the modulus is chosen at run time (prime bucket counts, configurable shard counts) and reused many times: it replaces a 32-bit div (README plot: about 0.86 s vs 0.25-0.30 s for 10^8 dependent remainders, roughly 3x).

Constant non-power-of-two 32-bit divisors on x64 where the compiler's quotient-then-subtract code is on the critical path: the plot shows LKK at or below Clang for most divisors from 2 to 64, up to about 1.7x at Clang's worst divisors.
Divisibility tests (n % d == 0) in hot loops: one multiply and one compare.
C or C++ on 64-bit targets (GCC/Clang with __uint128_t, MSVC x64 or ARM64) that wants a single dependency-free header.
when_not_to_use: Power-of-two divisors: use a mask; the plot shows both compiler and LKK collapse to about 0.02 s at 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, so there is nothing to gain.
Compile-time constant divisors where a few cycles do not matter: Clang's own code is slightly faster at divisors 5 and 6 in the plot and within a few percent at several others.
64-bit operands: the u64 functions are experimental, signed 64-bit functions do not exist (issue #14), and on MSVC ARM64 computeM_u64 runs a 64-step bit-by-bit division.
32-bit targets: the 32-bit path itself needs __uint128_t (GCC/Clang) or __umulh (MSVC x64/ARM64), so x86-32 and ARM32 builds are not supported.
SIMD lanes or 16-bit types: libdivide (not catalogued here) covers vector and 16-bit division.

integration.dependencies: none (stdint.h/stdbool.h in C, <cstdint> in C++, <intrin.h> on MSVC)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 or C++11 (constexpr functions with C++14 relaxed constexpr, disabled on MSVC); a 64-bit compiler with __uint128_t, or MSVC x64/ARM64 (64-bit functions need _MSC_VER >= 1923); CMake 3.16 for the optional package config
integration.platforms: 64-bit only: x86-64 and AArch64 with GCC or Clang, MSVC x64 and ARM64
integration.thread_safety: stateless pure functions; M is a plain integer that can be shared read-only across threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: results match % and / on 32-bit operands for supported divisors, but you call functions with a precomputed M instead of using the operators

gotchas: C++ template bug (found by reading include/fastmod.h at HEAD; not reported upstream): fastmod::fastmod<int32_t d>(x) passes the template divisor straight to fastmod_s32 as positive_d, which must be |d|. For a negative d the uint32_t conversion gives garbage: emulating the header's arithmetic, fastmod<-5>(7) returns 1717986916 instead of 2, and 24 of 30 sampled negative-divisor cases are wrong. No test (tests/unit.c, cppincludetest1/2.cpp) exercises the fastmod<d>/fastdiv<d> templates; the documented fastmod_s32(a, M, |d|) form is correct.

Unchecked preconditions: fastdiv_u32 with d = 1 returns 0 (issue #9; documented as requiring d > 1), signed fastdiv must avoid d in {-1, 1, INT32_MIN}, computeM_s32 cannot take INT32_MIN, and fastmod_s32 with d = -1 and a = INT32_MIN is undefined. Nothing asserts these at run time.
The README API list shows uint64_t/int64_t dividends, but the header takes uint32_t/int32_t, so a 64-bit argument is silently truncated to 32 bits; use the experimental fastmod_u64 for 64-bit values.

Evidence harness: the README plot comes from lemire/constantdivisionbenchmarks/hashbenches, which inlines its own copy of the LKK remainder with the divisor as a compile-time macro (not fastmod.h with a runtime divisor), times one process per variant and divisor with bash time (a single run, no repetitions), and checks only that the exit codes, the low 8 bits of the final seed, agree. The 64-bit benchmarks in tests/ (modnbenchmark, moddivnbenchmark) have no published results.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the category's siblings (xsimd, SLEEF, VDT, fmath and other SIMD or elementary-function libraries) do integer division, so fastmod is the pick for scalar 32-bit modulo, division or divisibility by a reused divisor. For SIMD lanes, 16-bit or signed 64-bit types, libdivide (not catalogued) is the usual alternative; the LKK paper's abstract reports beating libdivide by about 15% for most reused non-constant divisors (search snippet only).
verified_claims_summary: The README plot (Intel Skylake, clang -O3, Clang version and exact CPU not stated) times 10^8 dependent iterations of seed = (seed*31 + 27961) % D for divisors 2-64: the divide instruction through a volatile divisor takes about 0.86 s at every divisor, Clang's constant-divisor code about 0.26-0.44 s, and the LKK remainder about 0.25-0.30 s (read off the image), so roughly 3x over div and up to about 1.7x over Clang at its worst divisors, with no gain at powers of two and Clang slightly ahead at 5 and 6. The Software: Practice and Experience 2019 paper reports gains over compiler code of sometimes more than 25% on Skylake and Ryzen, and about 15% over libdivide for reused runtime divisors (abstract via search snippets only).
status_note: Active: CI and quick-test commits on 2026-03-31 and 2026-04-11, release 0.1.0 in July 2024, MSVC 64-bit support merged in November 2024, no open issues; an Apache-2.0 single header that is trivial to vendor, but avoid the C++ fastmod<d> template with negative divisors until it passes |d|.
